Question: Is there any other writing system that works like Chinese? It allows speakers of unrelated languages or distantly related languages to understand each other when writing, and modern people to understand 2000-3000 year old texts.
Answer: In terms of being a language family that enjoys unbroken continuity and in active use today? No. Yes, there are a number of ancient, pre-AD languages in use today. But they all suffer lock-in, because the written form, to a fault, spell sounds (or syllables) from a set of letters, also known as an alphabet. What is lock-in? The exclusive set of sounds and unique combinations that make up the spoken or oral language. For example, French and English are both spelled with latin letters, but knowledge of English does not allow one to read French, and vice versa, because the sound combinations are exclusive, with the exception of loan words. Written Chinese isn’t spelled. It is drawn. Chinese block writing obeys a simple rule. One block, one character, one sound (syllable). Each character represents a word with meaning. Each Chinese dialect overlays a separate, independent sound layer on the same set of characters, which allows a single script to be used across all dialects. How block writing unlocks the past is the unbroken logical foundations constantly being refined and updated with the times, allowing modern characters to share sufficient commonality with more ancient scripts to be decoded. More importantly, the ideas and databank from which they are drawn have been continuously maintained and expanded for millennium, allowing modern Chinese readers to draw from the same pool of knowledge.

Question: Why has the Malaysian Ringgit been depreciating against the Singapore dollar and the US dollar over the last 15 years?
Answer: I'll give a cliffsnotes version. Post GFC, the dollar depreciated massively, and it drove a nice commodity boom. The ringgit rode the wave and strengthened, while boosting export value due to the price boom. That's a rare occurrence, a sorta mini jackpot. 2012 changed all that, as the euro debt crisis flared, and subsequently, carte blanche was given to Japan to devalue the yen. Most of the third world followed suit, depreciating aggressively with one notable absentee—the Chinese yuan. It was this pivotal reverse plaza accord signed off by Barack that drove the massive expansion of trade, particularly Chinese imports from asean that doubled in the decade after 2012. Despite the healthy trade growth, Malaysia found itself unable to wean off fiscal deficits, with previous administrations having made cuts to the budget, leaving sacred cows on the table that couldn't be sacrificed. There are other issues but we don't have to discuss them. Structurally, the economy was set up to weaken the ringgit to help drive domestic growth, and it was exacerbated by the yen's decade long slide. It only reversed recently with the yen's uturn. The argument for a weak ringgit in the near term remains.

Question: Are China’s air and sea forces now capable of enforcing a blockade of Taiwan?
Answer: Let me point to a startling, but largely unreported development recently. The recently concluded Operation Joint Sword 2024A was announced and initialized WITHIN THE HOUR. In other words, this set of exclusion zones was enforced ON DEMAND. That’s an area spanning ~100,000 sq. km. This is a substantial upgrade in operational readiness and capability from the 2022 version, which I dub the Nancy drill. The Chinese took their time between announcement and initialization two years ago, but it’s the snap of a finger today, because of the preparations made, especially the deployment of force, the rerouting of civilian traffic and enforcement of exclusion zones. China rotates a steady stream of units to exercise around Taiwan year-round, in order to build experience, and keep up the military presence. This is exhausting the Taiwanese military to fatigue, having to constantly respond and challenge inbound contact. There have been accidents/losses on the Taiwanese side, but no serious incident reported from mainland units. This is a testament to the training, and upkeep of the frontline PLA, and highlights the gulf in capacity between the two sides. And where was the Reagan, the carrier that was in theater? Far south in the Philippine Sea, away from the action. Operation Joint Sword, studied carefully, reveal how sharp and lethal the Chinese have forged and reformed their doctrine and readiness. After all, 利剑’s literal meaning is Sharp Sword. So the answer is yes. And it’s not conjecture but demonstrated.

Question: Do you believe that Beijing can manage China's property crisis without it spilling over to the rest of the economy?
Answer: Certainly. First, China has extraordinary control over the price of goods in the economy, Why? The Chinese government has the world’s best stocked larder and warehouses for food and commodities. These are strategic, nationwide stockpiles painstakingly built up over decades, with SOEs keeping a watchful eye on supply. This is why China barely hiccuped when the swine flu decimated pig farming, or when covid necessitated repeated lockdowns. In other words, there is incredible stability built into the Chinese economy. Two, the days of raising expensive capital to chase property appreciation is no more, even in the lower tiers. Domestic lending criteria has tightened significantly, especially for big developers, and Xu Jiayin is in jail awaiting trial, the poster boy for profligate, and ultimately ruinous ambition. Foreign capital is staying away after the fallout, and the sector as a whole is being shunned by capital. Three, China has plenty of infrastructure to build or improve on, with >200m chinese in the queue for urbanization. Coupled with service improvements, these will drive real, organic growth in property prices for the next two decades, hopefully, in more realistic step with rising income. We live in a world where real estate in some Indian cities is more expensive than tier one cities in China today, so there is room for prices to rise tomorrow. Four, China has plenty of policy space to maneuver, because it hasn’t had to resort to GFC (and beyond) levels of policy support over covid, unlike the first world. The popping of the property bubble can therefore be cushioned through selective targeting of other economic sectors, without resorting to massive stimulus or extreme monetary policy. Real estate speculation is a humongous market worth trillions. It will take years of careful management to bring under control. But there are effective cards China hasn’t dealt, such as instituting a property tax. Note: GDP is transactional. Real estate is asset wealth.
